title: Waxing wroth
html_source:
Reference to Mutabilitie by Edmund Spenser
(Gifford).

It consists of two cantos which were not published in The Faerie Queen but assumed to be a part of it.

Spenser was an Elizabethan poet and took it upon himself to write and develop an English literary culture. The main product was the Faerie Queene, written for Queen Elizabeth and her court, hoping to emulate Virgil but firmly set in the Italian mould á la Arioso and Tasso.

In Mutabilitie, the titaness Mutabilitie interferes with the natural order. Jove attempts to restore the norm.

‘But to the highest Him, that is behight
Father of Gods and Men by equal Might;
To weet, the God of Nature, I appeal.
There-at Jove wexed wroth, and in his Spright’

However, Spenser also wrote a A view of the state of Ireland, an imagined dialog during which characters disparage the savage Irish and argue for brutal militarisation of a rebellious land. Eglington was a Presbyterian.
